title: Canadian time pressure and shrinking everyday friendship contact make social connection a scarce household resource
source_unit: Statistics Canada, Time Use Survey: time pressure and time spent with friends over the last 30 years
geography: Canada; non-institutionalized persons aged 15 years and older living in the provinces

denominator.unit: Canadian non-institutionalized persons aged 15 years and older in the Time Use Survey target population

women_high_time_pressure_2022.unit: percent of women+ reporting high time pressure

men_high_time_pressure_2022.unit: percent of men+ reporting high time pressure

mechanism.value: Time pressure operates as a hidden price on leisure, care, friendship, and cultural participation, with women reporting a higher burden than men

observations.method: Statistics Canada Time Use Survey cross-sectional waves from 1992 through 2022; high time pressure is defined as agreement with at least seven of ten time-pressure statements.
observations.uncertainty: The series compares repeated cross-sectional surveys rather than tracking the same people; the measure is self-reported and combines several dimensions of perceived time scarcity.
observations.subgroup: Canadian women+ and men+ categories as defined by Statistics Canada; historical sex/gender category construction is not identical across waves.
observations.counterinterpretation: The increase may reflect changing expectations, reporting norms, age structure, work and care composition, or survey context rather than a uniform increase in objectively constrained hours.

denominator.unit: Canadian non-institutionalized persons aged 15 years and older in the Time Use Survey target population

saw_friends_average_day_1986.unit: percent seeing friends on an average day

saw_friends_average_day_2022.unit: percent seeing friends on an average day

mechanism.value: Everyday social connection is becoming less frequent in the time diary, suggesting that friendship and belonging compete with work, care, commuting, digital activity, and household demands for scarce time

observations.method: Statistics Canada 24-hour time-diary measures of who was present during activities, compared across Time Use Survey waves from 1986 through 2022.
observations.uncertainty: Seeing a friend on the diary day is not the same as friendship quality, total monthly contact, online contact, loneliness, or social support; survey mode and life-cycle composition may affect comparisons.
observations.subgroup: Canadian persons aged 15 years and older in the survey target population; age-specific patterns are reported separately by the source.
observations.counterinterpretation: A decline in same-day in-person contact may coexist with stronger digital, household, workplace, or less frequent but more meaningful relationships; the measure cannot identify substitution.

denominator.unit: Canadian respondents who saw friends on the diary day, plus all survey respondents for unmet-time concern

average_hours_with_friends_1986.unit: hours per day among people who saw friends on the diary day

average_hours_with_friends_2022.unit: hours per day among people who saw friends on the diary day

average_hours_change.unit: hours per day change among people who saw friends on the diary day

worry_insufficient_family_friend_time_19.unit: percent reporting worry that they did not spend enough time with family and friends

worry_insufficient_family_friend_time_20.unit: percent reporting worry that they did not spend enough time with family and friends

mechanism.value: The social-time constraint appears at both margins: fewer people encounter friends on a given day, and those who do spend less time together, while concern about insufficient family and friendship time rises

observations.method: Statistics Canada combines diary-based duration among people who saw friends with survey responses on perceived insufficiency of family and friendship time.
observations.uncertainty: The duration statistic is conditional on seeing friends that day, while the worry measure has a different denominator; neither establishes loneliness, causal time displacement, or a mental-health outcome.
observations.subgroup: Canadian respondents in the Time Use Survey, with the source-specific conditional denominator for average hours.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower average duration may reflect a shift toward shorter, more distributed, or more digitally mediated contacts rather than a simple collapse in social connection.

related_sources.claim: Statistics Canada provides the underlying time-use tables for time pressure, time spent alone and with others, and related sociodemographic breakdowns.
Statistics Canada provides an interactive time-use visualization based on the 2022 Time Use Survey.

boundary: This record adds Canadian time-diary and perceived-time-pressure evidence on social connection, friendship contact, gendered time burden, and unmet family/friendship time. It does not measure cultural participation directly, online contact, loneliness, causal time displacement, or individual mental-health outcomes.
